screens.title: Constructors, Methods, and Instance Variables
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we assemble three core building blocks of Java objects: instance variables, methods, and constructors. You will learn what instance variables are and why each object keeps its own copy, how to protect those variables using private access and public getters and setters, and how constructors create objects with a well-defined initial state. We will also look closely at the this keyword — why it matters when parameter names shadow fields — and common mistakes such as losing the default constructor when you define a parameterized one. Learning these concepts matters because they let you model real-world entities safely and predictably. For example, by making a book's title private and exposing a setter that validates non-empty text, you prevent invalid state across your app. As you go through the lesson screens you'll see concise code examples, guided explanations of common pitfalls, and a short hands-on activity to practice adding constructors and encapsulation to a Book class. By the end you will be able to create well-initialized objects, control access to their state, and write clear methods that do one thing well.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Constructors, Methods, and Instance Variables
Constructors • Methods • State
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

We'll practice turning public attributes into private instance variables, adding getters and setters with validation, and writing constructors that guarantee a valid starting state. You'll see code examples and a short activity to update a Book class.

In this lesson
Instance variables & encapsulation
Why each object keeps its own state and how to protect it.
Coming up
Constructors & overloading
Default vs parameterized and how to initialize safely.
Practice
Hands-on Book class
Make fields private, add constructors, and validate inputs.
Quick preview
public class Dog {
  private String name;
  private int age;

  public Dog(String name, int age) {
    this.name = name;
    this.age = age;
  }

  public String getName() { return name; }
  public void setName(String name) { this.name = name; }

  public void bark() { System.out.println(name + " says Woof!"); }
}
Visual concept
Object state per instance
Each object gets its own copy of instance variables. Two Dog objects can have different ages and names even though they share one class blueprint.
buddy.name = "Buddy"

lucy.age = 5
Different objects, different state
Key Takeaway

Encapsulation plus constructors give you control: define where data lives, how it's set, and ensure objects start in a valid state.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives focus your practice on creating safe, well-initialized objects. First, you will define and initialize instance variables inside a class and understand that each object has its own copy. Second, you will create getter and setter methods to encapsulate access, using validation inside setters when appropriate. Third, you will understand constructors: how the no-argument default constructor works, and how parameterized constructors let you set initial state with new. Fourth, you will use the this keyword to refer to the current object's fields and, when appropriate, to call other constructors in the same class. Each objective is practical: for example, making a Book class's fields private and adding a parameterized constructor ensures every book created by your library code starts with a title and author. A common misconception is that getters and setters automatically make code safe — they only do so when you include validation or preserve invariants. By practicing these objectives you'll build objects that are easier to reason about and less likely to hold invalid state.

screens.title: Instance Variables — per-object state
screens.narratorSegment: An instance variable is a variable declared inside a class but outside any method or constructor, and each object created from that class receives its own copy. This means that two Dog objects can have different name and age values even though they share the same class blueprint. Conceptually, think of the class as a cookie cutter and each object as a cookie; instance variables are the icing applied differently to each cookie. In practice, you declare these variables in the class body, and you typically decide whether they should have explicit initial values or be initialized in a constructor. A common beginner mistake is to treat instance variables like global variables and make them public without thinking about invariants; that makes it hard to enforce rules like "age must be positive." For a concrete example, consider a Book class with private title, author, and isbn fields. Each Book object holds its own title string. If you want predictable behavior, initialize these fields in a constructor or with safe defaults. A key takeaway: instance variables represent the per-object state you model; design them so objects cannot enter invalid states by accident.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Instance Variables
Definition
A variable declared inside a class but outside methods or constructors. Each object has its own copy, so object state is independent across instances.
Example
public class Book {
  private String title; // instance variable
  private String author;
  private String isbn;
}
Why it matters
Independent state per object lets you model multiple real-world entities without interference.
Common mistake
Making fields public and letting code modify them directly removes opportunities for validation and leads to inconsistent state.
Visual: multiple objects with different state
bookA
title = "1984"
author = "George Orwell"
bookB
title = "The Hitchhiker's Guide"
author = "Douglas Adams"
Key Takeaway

Design instance variables carefully: they define what each object remembers. Prefer private fields and controlled initialization.

screens.title: Encapsulation: private fields and public accessors
screens.narratorSegment: Encapsulation is the practice of hiding an object's internal state and exposing a controlled interface. In Java this is commonly implemented by declaring instance variables as private and providing public getter and setter methods. Getters retrieve values safely while setters give you a place to add validation or normalization logic. For instance, a setAge method can check that an age value is positive before assigning it; doing so prevents invalid state across the program. A common error is leaving fields public and assuming clients will behave; that quickly becomes brittle when multiple places update the same field without rules. Another subtle point is that setters allow you to centralize logging or derived updates, such as recomputing a formatted name when parts change. Concretely, you'll practice converting public fields into private fields, adding getTitle and setTitle for a Book, and ensuring setTitle rejects empty strings. This design makes your objects easier to test and maintains invariants. As a learner question: where would you place validation that an ISBN matches a pattern — in the setter or before calling the setter? Generally the setter is the right place, because it enforces the rule for all callers.

keyIdea.text: Use private fields plus getters/setters to validate, normalize, and control access to object state.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Encapsulation
Public vs Private
Public field
Anyone can read and write directly. Easy but unsafe when invariants must be preserved.
Private + accessors
Controlled access. Validation, logging, and derived updates happen in one place.
Example: setter with validation
public void setAge(int age) {
  if (age > 0) {
    this.age = age;
  } else {
    System.out.println("Age cannot be zero or negative.");
  }
}
When to validate in a setter
  • Use setters to enforce rules every time a field changes.
  • Keep validation minimal and clear; throw or report errors consistently.
  • Prefer centralized rules in setters instead of duplicating checks across the codebase.
Pro tip

If a setter must perform heavy validation, consider factory methods or builder patterns for clearer construction APIs, but keep simple checks in setters.

screens.title: Getters and Setters — code walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete code example that shows getters and setters in action and why the this keyword is necessary. Start with private fields for name, breed, and age. A simple getter returns the value. A setter accepts a parameter and assigns it to the field; when the parameter has the same name as the field we must use this. field to refer to the instance variable. Otherwise the assignment will set the parameter to itself and the field remains unchanged. For example, this. name = name; makes it clear we update the object's name. The setAge method is a useful place for validation: check that age is positive before assigning. This prevents invalid state like negative ages. In the example code you'll see both getters and setters and a bark method that reads the name to print a message. As a learner exercise, remove this in a setter and predict the output: you will observe that the field does not change and the object keeps its previous value. That common mistake explains why this matters in everyday code.

keyIdea.text: Use this.field when a parameter shadows a field so the instance variable is updated correctly.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Getters & Setters
Code editor (read-only)
public class Dog {
  private String name;
  private String breed;
  private int age;

  // Getter for name
  public String getName() {
    return name;
  }

  // Setter for name
  public void setName(String name) {
    this.name = name; // 'this' refers to the instance variable
  }

  // Setter for age with validation
  public void setAge(int age) {
    if (age > 0) {
      this.age = age;
    } else {
      System.out.println("Age cannot be zero or negative.");
    }
  }

  public void bark() {
    System.out.println(name + " says Woof! Woof!");
  }
}
Explanation & checks
  • Getter: Returns the current value; no side effects.
  • Setter: Validates then assigns using this.field to avoid shadowing errors.
  • Validation: Keeps object in a valid state and centralizes checks.
Concrete scenario
Create a Dog with the no-argument constructor, call setName("Buddy"), then bark. If setName omitted this, name remains null and bark prints "null says Woof!" which demonstrates the bug.
Common mistake

Omitting this in setters with shadowed parameters leaves fields unchanged. Always check parameter names and field access during review.

screens.title: Constructors — purpose and rules
screens.narratorSegment: A constructor is a special method invoked automatically when you create an object with the new keyword. Its job is to initialize the object's instance variables so the object starts in a valid state. Constructors have the same name as the class and do not declare a return type. If you do not write any constructors, Java provides a default no-argument constructor that performs no special initialization. That is why earlier code used new Dog() without a defined constructor. However, once you define any constructor, the default is no longer provided; if you still need a no-argument option you must write it explicitly. Constructors can run simple setup code such as assigning default values and printing a message, but avoid heavy logic; complex setup can be moved to factory methods. A concrete example is adding a parameterized constructor to Dog that accepts name, breed, and age and assigns them using this. A common pitfall is giving the constructor a return type, which makes it a regular method rather than a constructor. Remember: constructor names must match the class exactly and must not include a return type.

keyIdea.text: Constructors set instance variables at creation; defining any constructor removes Java's automatic no-argument default.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Constructors
Why constructors matter
Constructors guarantee that every object you create starts with intended values. Without them, fields might remain null or uninitialized leaving the rest of the program to handle unexpected cases.
Example: parameterized and no-argument
public Dog() {
  this.name = "Unnamed";
  this.breed = "Unknown";
  this.age = 0;
  System.out.println("An unnamed dog has been created.");
}

public Dog(String name, String breed, int age) {
  this.name = name;
  this.breed = breed;
  this.age = age;
  System.out.println("A new dog named " + name + " has joined the kennel!");
}
Rules & pitfalls
  • Constructors share the class name exactly and have no return type.
  • Defining any constructor prevents Java from auto-creating a no-argument constructor.
  • Avoid heavy logic in constructors; prefer factory methods for complex setup.
Check your understanding

If you add a parameterized constructor, will new Dog() still compile? Only if you also define a no-argument constructor explicitly.

screens.title: Default vs Parameterized Constructors
screens.narratorSegment: Default and parameterized constructors serve different needs. A default constructor — the no-argument one — typically sets safe defaults, providing a simple way to create an object without supplying data. Java supplies a default no-argument constructor only when you have not defined any constructors. A parameterized constructor, in contrast, accepts arguments to initialize fields immediately, which is useful when you want an object to start with meaningful values. Consider creating a Book with a parameterized constructor that sets title, author, and isbn at construction time; that reduces later setter calls and keeps the object valid earlier. If you need both behaviors, define both constructors explicitly. Constructor overloading means you can have multiple constructors with different parameter lists to support different use cases. A common misuse is defining only a parameterized constructor, then attempting to call new Class() elsewhere — compilation will fail because the default no-argument constructor no longer exists. Use defaults for convenience and parameterized constructors to enforce required data at creation time. Default vs Parameterized Constructors means use parameterized constructors to require essential data; provide no-argument constructors when convenience defaults are helpful.. In practical terms, compare behaviors and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Default vs Parameterized
Default / No-argument

Supplied automatically only when no constructors are declared. Usually sets safe defaults or leaves fields null depending on design.

Example
public Book() { this.title = "Untitled"; this.author = "Unknown"; }
Parameterized

Accepts arguments to initialize fields immediately. Encourages creating valid objects from the start.

Example
public Book(String title, String author, String isbn) {
  this.title = title;
  this.author = author;
  this.isbn = isbn;
}
Key Takeaway

If both behaviors are needed, declare both constructors explicitly. Remember that defining any constructor removes Java's automatic default.

screens.title: Constructor Overloading and this() calls
screens.narratorSegment: Constructor overloading is having multiple constructors with different parameter lists so callers can create objects in different ways. For example you could have a no-argument constructor that sets defaults and a parameterized constructor that accepts full details. To avoid duplicating initialization logic, one constructor can call another using this(...) with appropriate arguments. That lets you centralize setup in one place and keep other constructors as thin wrappers. For instance, a no-argument constructor might call this("Untitled","Unknown","N/A") so the parameterized constructor performs the assignments and any shared side-effects. Note that this(...) must be the first statement in the constructor. A common mistake is trying to call this(...) after other code in the constructor, which causes a compile-time error. Overloading gives flexibility to callers while ensuring consistent initialization paths. When designing overloaded constructors, prefer the most complete constructor as the central place for validation and side-effects so all creation paths enforce the same invariants. Constructor Overloading and this() calls means use overloaded constructors with this(...) to centralize initialization and avoid duplicated assignment logic.. In practical terms, provide multiple ways to construct an object and reuse initialization code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Overloading & this()
Example: reuse initialization
public Book() {
  this("Untitled", "Unknown Author", "N/A");
}

public Book(String title, String author, String isbn) {
  this.title = title;
  this.author = author;
  this.isbn = isbn;
  System.out.println("Book '" + title + "' created.");
}
Note that this(...) must be the first statement. Centralize validation and side effects in the most complete constructor so all constructors share the same behavior.
Common pitfall
Calling this(...) after other code causes a compile-time error. Use this(...) as the first line to delegate construction responsibilities.
Check
If you need both convenience defaults and parameterized creation with validation, delegate from simple constructors to the full one using this(...).

screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Developers often make a small set of recurring mistakes with methods and constructors. First, forgetting to declare a return type for a non-constructor method turns it into a constructor-like declaration or causes a compile error; all non-constructor methods must specify a return type such as void, int, or String. Second, giving a constructor a return type accidentally makes it a method, not a constructor — the code will compile differently and object creation won't call that method. Third, misusing the this keyword in setters or constructors by omitting it when a parameter shadows a field will leave the field unchanged. A simple debugging pattern is to create short tests in main that construct an object and call methods that print state; comparing expected and observed output quickly reveals these issues. For example, create a Dog with new Dog(), call setName("Buddy") and then call bark(); if bark prints null says Woof!, you likely forgot this in the setter. These small checks are effective, and writing unit tests for constructors and setter validation prevents regressions. Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Common Mistakes
Quick test pattern
public class Kennel {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    Dog d = new Dog();
    d.setName("Buddy");
    d.bark(); // Expect: Buddy says Woof! Woof!
  }
}
If the output shows null instead of Buddy, inspect the setter for missing this or shadowing issues. If new Dog() fails to compile after adding a parameterized constructor, add an explicit no-argument constructor if you need it.
Checklist
  • Non-constructor methods must declare a return type.
  • Constructors must match the class name and have no return type.
  • Use this when parameters shadow fields.
  • Write small runtime checks to validate constructor and setter behavior.
Common bug
Defining a constructor but forgetting a no-argument one breaks code that calls new Class() elsewhere. Always update call sites or restore a no-argument constructor.

screens.title: Designing methods and behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Methods are how objects express behavior and interact with other parts of the program. When designing a method, decide its purpose, its input parameters, and what it returns. Non-constructor methods must specify a return type; use void for actions with no result, or a specific type when computing and returning a value. A good design principle is single responsibility: each method should do one thing well. For example, a Dog's bark method prints a message and does not return a value; a BankAccount deposit method modifies balance and should include validation to ensure the deposit is positive. That deposit example from the assessment shows encapsulation: balance remains private and only the deposit method changes it after checking the amount. Also consider side effects and whether a method should throw an exception on invalid input or print an error. Prefer returning error signals or throwing exceptions for libraries and reserve printing for quick demos. Finally, document any validation rules so callers know how to use methods correctly and tests can assert expected behaviors. Designing methods and behavior means give methods clear purpose, declare return types, validate parameters, and keep side effects understandable.. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we assemble three core building blocks of Java objects: instance variables, methods, and constructors. You will learn what instance variables are and why each object keeps its own copy, how to protect those variables using private access and public getters and setters, and how constructors create objects with a well-defined initial state. We will also look closely at the this keyword — why it matters when parameter names shadow fields — and common mistakes such as losing the default constructor when you define a parameterized one. Learning these concepts matters because they let you model real-world entities safely and predictably. For example, by making a book's title private and exposing a setter that validates non-empty text, you prevent invalid state across your app. As you go through the lesson screens you'll see concise code examples, guided explanations of common pitfalls, and a short hands-on activity to practice adding constructors and encapsulation to a Book class. By the end you will be able to create well-initialized objects, control access to their state, and write clear methods that do one thing well.

These four objectives focus your practice on creating safe, well-initialized objects. First, you will define and initialize instance variables inside a class and understand that each object has its own copy. Second, you will create getter and setter methods to encapsulate access, using validation inside setters when appropriate. Third, you will understand constructors: how the no-argument default constructor works, and how parameterized constructors let you set initial state with new. Fourth, you will use the this keyword to refer to the current object's fields and, when appropriate, to call other constructors in the same class. Each objective is practical: for example, making a Book class's fields private and adding a parameterized constructor ensures every book created by your library code starts with a title and author. A common misconception is that getters and setters automatically make code safe — they only do so when you include validation or preserve invariants. By practicing these objectives you'll build objects that are easier to reason about and less likely to hold invalid state.

This second objectives screen shows how you'll practice each skill. First, when you define instance variables you will decide sensible defaults or explicit initialization in constructors to prevent nulls or invalid values. Second, getters will be simple read methods while setters can include validation logic; for example, a setAge method should reject non-positive numbers. Third, when writing constructors you'll practice a no-argument constructor that sets defaults and a parameterized constructor that accepts explicit values; you'll see how defining any constructor removes Java's automatic default, so add a no-argument one if you still need it. Fourth, using this ensures that parameters with the same name as fields update the intended member; you'll also try calling another constructor from one constructor to reuse initialization code. These practical exercises map directly to the hands-on activity: update your Book class, add both constructors, and verify the validation behaves as expected. Expect to test with both constructors so you can see default and custom initialization in action.

An instance variable is a variable declared inside a class but outside any method or constructor, and each object created from that class receives its own copy. This means that two Dog objects can have different name and age values even though they share the same class blueprint. Conceptually, think of the class as a cookie cutter and each object as a cookie; instance variables are the icing applied differently to each cookie. In practice, you declare these variables in the class body, and you typically decide whether they should have explicit initial values or be initialized in a constructor. A common beginner mistake is to treat instance variables like global variables and make them public without thinking about invariants; that makes it hard to enforce rules like "age must be positive." For a concrete example, consider a Book class with private title, author, and isbn fields. Each Book object holds its own title string. If you want predictable behavior, initialize these fields in a constructor or with safe defaults. A key takeaway: instance variables represent the per-object state you model; design them so objects cannot enter invalid states by accident.

Encapsulation is the practice of hiding an object's internal state and exposing a controlled interface. In Java this is commonly implemented by declaring instance variables as private and providing public getter and setter methods. Getters retrieve values safely while setters give you a place to add validation or normalization logic. For instance, a setAge method can check that an age value is positive before assigning it; doing so prevents invalid state across the program. A common error is leaving fields public and assuming clients will behave; that quickly becomes brittle when multiple places update the same field without rules. Another subtle point is that setters allow you to centralize logging or derived updates, such as recomputing a formatted name when parts change. Concretely, you'll practice converting public fields into private fields, adding getTitle and setTitle for a Book, and ensuring setTitle rejects empty strings. This design makes your objects easier to test and maintains invariants. As a learner question: where would you place validation that an ISBN matches a pattern — in the setter or before calling the setter? Generally the setter is the right place, because it enforces the rule for all callers.

Let's walk through a concrete code example that shows getters and setters in action and why the this keyword is necessary. Start with private fields for name, breed, and age. A simple getter returns the value. A setter accepts a parameter and assigns it to the field; when the parameter has the same name as the field we must use this. field to refer to the instance variable. Otherwise the assignment will set the parameter to itself and the field remains unchanged. For example, this. name = name; makes it clear we update the object's name. The setAge method is a useful place for validation: check that age is positive before assigning. This prevents invalid state like negative ages. In the example code you'll see both getters and setters and a bark method that reads the name to print a message. As a learner exercise, remove this in a setter and predict the output: you will observe that the field does not change and the object keeps its previous value. That common mistake explains why this matters in everyday code.

A constructor is a special method invoked automatically when you create an object with the new keyword. Its job is to initialize the object's instance variables so the object starts in a valid state. Constructors have the same name as the class and do not declare a return type. If you do not write any constructors, Java provides a default no-argument constructor that performs no special initialization. That is why earlier code used new Dog() without a defined constructor. However, once you define any constructor, the default is no longer provided; if you still need a no-argument option you must write it explicitly. Constructors can run simple setup code such as assigning default values and printing a message, but avoid heavy logic; complex setup can be moved to factory methods. A concrete example is adding a parameterized constructor to Dog that accepts name, breed, and age and assigns them using this. A common pitfall is giving the constructor a return type, which makes it a regular method rather than a constructor. Remember: constructor names must match the class exactly and must not include a return type.

Default and parameterized constructors serve different needs. A default constructor — the no-argument one — typically sets safe defaults, providing a simple way to create an object without supplying data. Java supplies a default no-argument constructor only when you have not defined any constructors. A parameterized constructor, in contrast, accepts arguments to initialize fields immediately, which is useful when you want an object to start with meaningful values. Consider creating a Book with a parameterized constructor that sets title, author, and isbn at construction time; that reduces later setter calls and keeps the object valid earlier. If you need both behaviors, define both constructors explicitly. Constructor overloading means you can have multiple constructors with different parameter lists to support different use cases. A common misuse is defining only a parameterized constructor, then attempting to call new Class() elsewhere — compilation will fail because the default no-argument constructor no longer exists. Use defaults for convenience and parameterized constructors to enforce required data at creation time. Default vs Parameterized Constructors means use parameterized constructors to require essential data; provide no-argument constructors when convenience defaults are helpful.. In practical terms, compare behaviors and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Constructor overloading is having multiple constructors with different parameter lists so callers can create objects in different ways. For example you could have a no-argument constructor that sets defaults and a parameterized constructor that accepts full details. To avoid duplicating initialization logic, one constructor can call another using this(...) with appropriate arguments. That lets you centralize setup in one place and keep other constructors as thin wrappers. For instance, a no-argument constructor might call this("Untitled","Unknown","N/A") so the parameterized constructor performs the assignments and any shared side-effects. Note that this(...) must be the first statement in the constructor. A common mistake is trying to call this(...) after other code in the constructor, which causes a compile-time error. Overloading gives flexibility to callers while ensuring consistent initialization paths. When designing overloaded constructors, prefer the most complete constructor as the central place for validation and side-effects so all creation paths enforce the same invariants.
